claims.text: Inflation is low by historical standards [September 2026]
claims.note: Headline CPI rose 3.7% in the 12 months to September 2026, above every reading in 2024 (max 3.5%) and 2025 (2.3-3.0%) and above the 2019-20 pre-pandemic pace of about 1.5-2.5%; only the 2021-23 spike (peak 9.1% in June 2022) and April-May 2026 (3.8%, 4.2%) were higher in this series.

claims.text: Inflation today is substantially below its peak under the previous administration
claims.note: The 12-month CPI-U change peaked at 9.1% in June 2022 and was 3.7% in September 2026, less than half the peak.

claims.text: The previous administration presided over the worst inflation in US history
claims.note: The 2022 peak of 9.1 percent was the highest since 1981 but below the 14.8 percent of 1980 and the near-20 percent of 1947.

claims.text: Gasoline prices will return to their pre-war level when the Iran conflict ends
claims.note: A prediction; oil fell quickly after the 1991 Gulf War, but markets may price in a lasting Gulf risk premium and pump prices fall more slowly than they rise.

claims.text: Tariffs do not raise consumer prices
claims.note: The staff report estimates that about 26 percent of a tariff increase passes through to consumer goods prices within a year, 64 percent directly via imported goods and 36 percent via domestically produced goods, and concludes the 2025 tariffs had economically and statistically significant effects on consumer prices.

claims.text: Tariffs make the country that imposes them wealthier
claims.note: The 2018-2019 tariffs produced a net welfare loss after counting revenue (Fajgelbaum et al.), and large majorities of surveyed economists say tariffs lower average living standards.

claims.text: Tariffs lead foreign manufacturers to build plants in the US to avoid them
claims.note: Tariff-jumping investment is a real mechanism (Japanese auto plants in the 1980s), but announced pledges far exceed realized spending and tariffs on inputs deter other investment.

claims.text: Tariffs have triggered a record wave of factory construction in the US [2026]
claims.note: Manufacturing construction spending peaked in 2024 on CHIPS and IRA projects and has since declined, and manufacturing employment fell through 2025; pledges are not spending.

claims.text: Tariff revenue is large enough to fund a cash payment to every adult citizen
claims.note: Tariffs bring in roughly 300-400 billion dollars a year while a 5,000 dollar payment to about 260 million adults would cost about 1.3 trillion dollars.

claims.text: Recent economic growth has raised the purchasing power of typical workers
claims.note: Real average hourly earnings for all employees fell 0.7% from September 2025 to September 2026 (nominal pay +3.0% vs CPI +3.7%), so the typical worker's purchasing power declined over the past year rather than rose.

claims.text: Lumber tariffs keep US sawmills operating at only a small cost to lumber buyers
claims.note: Protection does shift some output to domestic mills, but NAHB estimates lumber tariffs add thousands of dollars to a new home and US lumber output has been flat with weak housing starts.

claims.text: Tariffs are paid by the importing country's consumers and businesses, not by the exporter
claims.note: Regressions on HTS10-country import data through November 2025 find 94 percent of the tariff incidence fell on U.S. importers in January-August 2025 and 86 percent in November; a 10 percent tariff lowered foreign export prices only 0.6 to 1.4 percent, so U.S. firms and consumers bear the bulk of the burden.

claims.text: Foreign exporters absorb most of the cost of US import tariffs
claims.note: Foreign exporters bore only 6 to 14 percent of the 2025 tariff incidence by period, with U.S. importers bearing 86 to 94 percent; the staff report's import-price regressions give the same roughly 90 percent border pass-through.

claims.text: Tariffs raise the prices of domestically produced goods as well as imports
claims.note: The paper's central finding is that tariffs raise the prices of goods made at home, not just the imports they tax: 36 percent of the consumer price effect comes through domestic producers' higher imported-input costs and higher markups under weaker import competition.

claims.text: Tariffs on inputs cost more jobs in the industries that use them than they protect in the producing industry
claims.note: Flaaen and Pierce (Fed, 2019) found the 2018-2019 tariffs' input-cost and retaliation effects outweighed import protection, for a net loss of manufacturing jobs.

claims.text: Steel tariffs boosted domestic steel investment and jobs at only a small cost in higher steel prices
claims.note: The USITC found the Section 232 tariffs raised domestic steel output and prices modestly, but the same report found larger output losses in steel-using industries.

claims.text: The 2018-2019 tariffs did not raise overall US consumer inflation
claims.note: Tariffed goods rose 10-30 percent in price but were a small share of the basket, so the aggregate CPI effect was a few tenths of a point, hard to see in headline figures.

claims.text: Retaliation and uncertainty from tariffs slow investment and growth
claims.note: Fed research (Caldara et al. 2020) estimated 2018-2019 trade-policy uncertainty cut US investment by about 1 percent, and retaliation cut farm and manufacturing exports.

claims.text: Tariffs cannot raise enough revenue to replace the income tax because high rates shrink imports
claims.note: Imports are about 3 trillion dollars against roughly 2.2 trillion of income tax revenue, and rates high enough to close the gap would cut imports sharply; PWBM and Tax Foundation reach the same conclusion.

claims.text: Tariff revenue and domestic investment offset the costs tariffs impose on consumers
claims.note: Rebating tariff revenue returns the transfer part of the cost, but Fajgelbaum et al. found the 2018-2019 tariffs still left a net loss after revenue because of deadweight and retaliation losses.

claims.text: The Smoot-Hawley tariff worsened the Great Depression
claims.note: Most economic historians rate Smoot-Hawley and the retaliation it triggered as a secondary factor that deepened the Depression by collapsing trade, with monetary contraction as the main cause.

claims.text: The Iran conflict has materially raised US gasoline prices
claims.note: Weekly regular gasoline stepped from 3.015 (03/02/2026) to 3.502 (03/09) and 3.990 (03/30), reaching 4.500 by 05/11, a 54% rise over the Feb 2026 pre-war monthly baseline of 2.908, in the same weeks WTI jumped from 64.51 (Feb) to 91.38 (Mar); the timing fits the conflict as the cause, though a price series alone cannot rule out other drivers.

claims.text: Short-run oil demand is so inelastic that a small supply loss causes a disproportionately large price spike
claims.note: Estimates of short-run oil demand elasticity cluster near -0.1, so a supply cut of a few percent implies a price move of tens of percent.

claims.text: Pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz cushion the loss of supply when the strait closes
claims.note: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline (about 5 million barrels a day to Yanbu) and the UAE's Habshan-Fujairah line can carry a large share of Gulf exports around the strait.

claims.text: Traders' expectations move oil prices ahead of actual changes in supply and demand
claims.note: In a calibrated model of geopolitical oil-supply risk, a rise in the probability of a production disaster raises the oil price through precautionary inventory demand even when no disaster occurs (about 4% for a 10pp shock to 9% for a 40pp shock), consistent with the 1979 and 1990 episodes; a model result, not a direct test of trader behaviour.

claims.text: Withdrawal of war-risk insurance can halt tanker traffic even where ships could physically pass
claims.note: Tankers cannot sail uninsured, and Joint War Committee listings with 72-hour cancellation have stopped traffic in the Red Sea and Black Sea in recent years.

claims.text: Oil prices will stay above their pre-war level after the Iran conflict because markets now price in Gulf supply risk
claims.note: The paper shows markets price the probability of a Gulf supply disruption (the June 2025 Iran-Israel war lifted the Hormuz-closure probability 13 points and the oil price 9%), but it calls that rise temporary and models the premium as fading with the probability, so it supports the risk-pricing mechanism without showing that prices stay above pre-war levels once a conflict ends.

claims.text: Gasoline prices are falling [spring 2026]
claims.note: The NSA gasoline index rose 24.9% in March, 11.1% in April and 8.6% in May 2026 (254.887 in January to 396.961 in May), a 56% rise over spring; it only began falling in June (-9.7%).

claims.text: Gasoline is cheaper now than it was under the previous administration [spring 2026]
claims.note: Spring 2026 (Mar-May) regular gasoline averaged 4.073 (3.638, 4.103, 4.479), 17.7% above the Biden-period (Feb 2021-Jan 2025) mean of 3.461 and 17.4% below the Biden peak of 4.929 (Jun 2022); April and May 2026 were each above the Biden mean, so gasoline was dearer than the typical Biden-era price, cheaper only than the 2022 peak.

claims.text: Gasoline prices rise quickly after an oil shock but fall back slowly
claims.note: In daily and weekly US station prices for 2002-2009, the rockets-and-feathers asymmetry is strongest from wholesale (rack and spot) to retail, where retail rises more than four times as fast as it falls, but it is statistically gone after about seven to ten days, and from crude oil to gasoline prices it is weak or even reversed, so the slow fall is real but short-lived and sits in the retail margin rather than in the response to crude.

claims.text: Rising diesel prices raise the cost of most other goods
claims.note: Diesel powers freight and farming, so its cost feeds into shipping and food prices, though fuel is only a few percent of most goods' final price.

claims.text: Being a net oil exporter does not shield US consumers from global oil price spikes
claims.note: US pump prices moved fully with the global crude shock: regular gasoline rose from 2.908 (Feb 2026) to 4.479 (May 2026), +54%, while WTI rose 58%, repeating the 2022 pattern (+40% gasoline, Feb-Jun); the series show consumers were not shielded but do not themselves state the US net-export position.

claims.text: Spring refinery maintenance and the switch to summer gasoline push pump prices up seasonally
claims.note: The monthly table shows the seasonal pattern the claim describes: May was higher than January in 15 of the 16 years 2010-2025 (e.g. 2024 3.075 to 3.603, 2019 2.248 to 2.859), but the series cannot separate refinery maintenance and summer-blend costs from demand or crude moves as the cause.

claims.text: Core inflation is a better guide to the underlying trend than headline inflation
claims.note: Core inflation forecasts future headline inflation better than headline does, which is why the Fed watches it, but it understates the cost of living when energy stays high.

claims.text: Gasoline prices are the main driver of the recent rise in headline inflation [September 2026]
claims.note: BLS reports the gasoline index rose 9.1% in September 2026 and accounted for over half of the 0.6% monthly all-items increase; over 12 months energy rose 20.4% due in large part to gasoline rising 34.2%.

claims.text: Monthly inflation has accelerated for several consecutive months [autumn 2026]
claims.note: Seasonally adjusted monthly all-items CPI changes ran -0.4% (June), 0.1% (July), 0.4% (August), 0.6% (September 2026): three consecutive months of acceleration.

claims.text: Grocery prices have been flat to falling while energy drives inflation [September 2026]
claims.note: Food at home changed -0.1%, 0.0% and -0.1% in July-September 2026 while energy rose 5.2% in September and gasoline accounted for over half the monthly all-items rise; grocery prices are still up 1.8% over 12 months, so flat-to-falling describes recent months, not the year.

claims.text: Inflation is caused by the government creating more money
claims.note: Sustained inflation needs monetary accommodation, but the 2021-2022 and 2026 episodes were driven largely by supply shocks in goods and energy, and money growth tracks prices poorly at short horizons.

claims.text: Bitcoin's fixed supply makes it a hedge against currency inflation
claims.note: The supply cap is real, but Bitcoin fell about 65 percent in 2022 while CPI peaked and trades like a risk asset, so it has not protected purchasing power over inflationary stretches.

claims.text: Importers absorb much of a new tariff at first and pass it to consumers over the following months
claims.note: Import prices rise almost one for one in the first month, so importers pay the tariff immediately, while retail pass-through of the direct effect is only about half complete after three months and full after six, and the indirect effect via domestic producers keeps building to twelve months.

claims.text: The 2025 tariffs are the largest US tax increase in decades as a share of the economy
claims.note: Tax Foundation and Yale Budget Lab both put the 2025 tariffs near 1 percent of GDP, the largest increase since 1993, though court rulings have since trimmed them.

claims.text: Tariffs have measurably raised US core inflation [2026]
claims.note: Tariffs contributed about 2.9 percentage points to twelve-month inflation in the 67 non-oil consumer goods categories sampled by February 2026, but the estimate is a relative-price effect identified against less-exposed goods and covers goods only (20 percent of the basket), so it does not measure the effect on core CPI as a whole.

claims.text: The US average effective tariff rate reached its highest level since the 1930s [2025]
claims.note: The paper states the 2025 tariffs took U.S. import tariffs to their highest levels since the 1930s, with the average statutory rate peaking near 16 percent in September 2025; the duty rate actually collected ran at about two-thirds of the statutory rate.

claims.text: The Iran war has raised US household borrowing costs through higher inflation and bond yields
claims.note: An oil shock lifts inflation expectations and Treasury yields, which feed mortgage and card rates; the size rests on Moody's model, which is not independently checked here.

claims.text: Airlines pass higher jet fuel costs to passengers through fares and fees
claims.note: Airline fares rose 22.4% in the 12 months to September 2026 (1.2% in the month) while fuel oil rose 74.2% and energy 20.4%, consistent with fuel costs passing into fares; the release reports the co-movement without attributing it.

claims.text: Real wages have fallen as inflation outpaced pay growth [2026]
claims.note: Real average hourly earnings decreased 0.7% from September 2025 to September 2026 (seasonally adjusted) as CPI growth outpaced nominal earnings growth; real weekly earnings fell 0.1%.

claims.text: Strong employment and GDP growth can coexist with falling household purchasing power
claims.note: In 2026 real hourly earnings fell 0.7% over the year while real GDP grew 2.5% and 2.2% annualized in Q1 and Q2 and unemployment held at 4.1-4.3%, showing growth and falling purchasing power coexisting; but job gains were weak (+29,000 in September, 45,000/month average), so the employment side was steady rather than strong.

claims.text: Gasoline has been above four dollars a gallon on more days this year than in any previous year [2026]
claims.note: Counting weekly national-average readings at or above 4.00 as a proxy for days, 2026 has 24 such weeks through 10/12 (Apr-May 8, Jun 3, Jul 2, Aug 5, Sep 4, Oct 2) against 23 in all of 2022 (Mar 7 to Aug 8) and 7 in 2008, so 2026 already exceeds every prior year with eleven weeks still to run; the national weekly average is a proxy, not a daily count.

claims.text: Over recent decades US real hourly pay has grown only slowly, with frequent down years
claims.note: BLS production-worker earnings deflated by CPI rose about 23 percent from 1990 to 2026, about 0.6 percent a year, with a third of years negative.

claims.text: Real wages fell during the 2021-2023 inflation spike before recovering as inflation cooled
claims.note: Derived real average hourly earnings growth was negative every month from April 2021 (-3.4%) through April 2023 (-0.3%), bottoming at -3.3% in June 2022, and turned positive from May 2023 (+0.2%) onward as CPI inflation fell below nominal wage growth.

claims.text: Average wage figures can rise because low-wage jobs disappear rather than because pay increased
claims.note: In April 2020 average hourly earnings jumped 4.6% in one month (to 8.1% year over year) while private employment fell 15.3% (about 19.6 million jobs, concentrated in low-wage sectors), the textbook composition effect the claim describes; the series show the pattern though they do not decompose it.

claims.text: Cumulative inflation has cut the purchasing power of a dollar held since 1990 by more than half
claims.note: CPI-U rose about 163 percent from January 1990 to 2026, so a 1990 dollar buys about 38 cents of goods.

claims.text: Importers stockpiled goods ahead of the tariffs, delaying the pass-through to consumer prices
claims.note: US imports surged to a record in early 2025 as firms front-ran announced tariffs, and inventories were run down through the year.

claims.text: Tariffs on Brazilian goods are the main cause of the recent spike in US beef and coffee prices [early 2026]
claims.note: The 50 percent Brazil tariff added to coffee and beef costs, but coffee was already up sharply on Brazilian drought and beef on a cyclically small US cattle herd and import restrictions.

claims.text: Tariffs strengthen the dollar enough to offset much of their cost to US buyers
claims.note: The dollar depreciated about 2 percent around the Liberation Day announcement rather than appreciating, and adding the exchange rate to the import-price regression leaves tariff pass-through at about 90 percent, so no exchange-rate offset is found.

claims.text: Owners' equivalent rent measures a housing cost that no one actually pays
claims.note: OER is imputed rather than paid in cash, but it is the standard way to measure the consumption value of owner-occupied housing and tracks market rents with a lag.

claims.text: The 2018-2019 tariffs left the US economy worse off even after counting tariff revenue
claims.note: Fajgelbaum et al. (2020) estimated consumer losses of about 69 billion against 61 billion of revenue plus producer gains, a net loss near 7 billion a year.

claims.text: Retaliation against US tariffs cut farm exports enough to require federal bailouts of farmers
claims.note: China's retaliatory tariffs cut US soybean exports sharply in 2018 and the USDA paid about 23 billion dollars in Market Facilitation Program aid in 2018-2019.

claims.text: Most academic economists hold that tariffs leave the average American worse off
claims.note: IGM Forum panels in 2018 and 2024 showed large majorities disagreeing that tariffs improve Americans' welfare.

claims.text: Tariffs raise government revenue while raising costs for US consumers
claims.note: Duties collected lifted the average duty rate to around 8.5 percent of import value while 86 to 94 percent of the tariff incidence fell on U.S. importers, so import prices for tariffed goods rose about 11 percent more than untariffed ones; revenue and higher U.S. costs arrive together.

claims.text: The Iran conflict has sharply raised US diesel and heating oil prices [2026]
claims.note: US No 2 diesel went from 3.722 in Feb 2026 to 4.921 in Mar, 5.600 in May and 6.291 in Sep (+69% over the pre-war month), the jump coinciding with the March 2026 crude spike; heating oil is not in this series and the attribution rests on timing.

claims.text: Monetary tightening does little to curb inflation caused by an oil supply shock
claims.note: Rate hikes work on demand and cannot add oil supply, though they can anchor expectations and limit second-round effects, as the Fed argued in 2022.

claims.text: Inflation was falling toward the Fed's target before the Iran war pushed it back up [2026]
claims.note: Headline CPI fell from 3.0% (September 2025) to 2.4% in January and February 2026, then jumped to 3.3%, 3.8% and 4.2% in March-May as the gasoline index rose 24.9% in March alone; the series confirm the fall and the energy-driven rebound, while the attribution to the Iran conflict comes from outside these documents.

claims.text: Price increases have broadened beyond energy into most CPI categories [September 2026]
claims.note: In September 2026 most major indexes rose (recreation, used cars, education, airline fares, medical care, apparel) and only a small number such as communication fell, and core CPI edged up to 2.6% from 2.4%; but core goods were up only 0.7% over the year and the core monthly rate was unchanged at 0.3%, so the broadening is modest rather than most categories accelerating.

claims.text: The 2025 US tariffs did not produce the inflation spike that economists predicted
claims.note: Tariffs lifted consumer goods inflation in the sample from slightly negative to about 2 percent, a 2.9 point contribution spread over a year rather than a sudden spike; the post does not compare this to any economist forecasts and covers goods only.

claims.text: Tariffs are now a major source of federal revenue
claims.note: Customs receipts ran about 30 billion dollars a month in late 2025, roughly 5 percent of federal revenue and several times the pre-2025 level.

claims.text: The tariffs did not push the US economy into recession [2025]
claims.note: Private employment grew every quarter of 2025 (134.7 million in January to 135.1 million in December) and unemployment stayed between 4.0% and 4.5%, so no recession occurred in 2025; the series say nothing about tariffs' role either way.

claims.text: The US has been among the fastest growing economies in the OECD [2025]
claims.note: US growth near 2 percent in 2025 led the G7 and beat the OECD average of about 1.5 percent.

claims.text: Memory-chip prices are feeding through into consumer electronics prices [2026]
claims.note: DRAM and NAND contract prices rose sharply from late 2025 on AI data-center demand, lifting PC and phone prices.

claims.text: Hotter-than-expected core inflation raises the odds of a Fed rate hike [autumn 2026]
claims.note: A forecast of Fed behaviour; depends on Fed guidance and later data.

claims.text: Gasoline prices have reached their highest level since the 2022 spike [spring 2026]
claims.note: May 2026 regular gasoline averaged 4.479, the highest monthly price since July 2022 (4.559); no month between Aug 2022 (3.975) and Feb 2026 exceeded 3.840 (Aug 2023), and the weekly 4.500 on 05/11/2026 was the highest since 07/18/2022 (4.490).

claims.text: A worldwide trade war reduces international trade and leaves every country worse off
claims.note: Retaliatory tariff rounds in the 1930s and 2018-2019 cut trade volumes and produced net losses for both sides in the studies that measured them.

claims.text: Tariffs used briefly as bargaining leverage do far less harm than tariffs kept as long-run policy
claims.note: Prolonged protection compounds the losses, but 2018-2019 studies found trade-policy uncertainty itself cut investment even when tariffs were short-lived or merely threatened.

claims.text: Whether tariffs raise the overall price level depends on how the Federal Reserve responds
claims.note: A tariff is an indirect tax whose wedge is resolved through higher prices or lower nominal incomes, and monetary policy determines which; in 2025 the Fed chose to look through it.

claims.text: Tariffs fall more heavily on lower-income households as a share of their income
claims.note: Lower-income households spend a larger share of income, and more of it on traded goods, so distributional analyses of broad tariffs consistently find a regressive burden.

claims.text: Tariffs on imported inputs raise costs for domestic manufacturers
claims.note: The marginal cost channel is the main route into domestic prices: for the average consumer goods industry, which uses 18 percent imported inputs, a 10 percent increase in input duties raises producer prices by 2.6 percent over twelve months, positive and significant in every specification.

claims.text: The economic burden tariffs impose on households exceeds the revenue they raise
claims.note: Tariffs create deadweight loss as buyers substitute toward pricier domestic goods, so estimated consumer costs exceeded collected revenue in studies of the 2018 tariffs.

claims.text: Tariffs reduce household real income whether the cost shows up as higher prices or lower nominal incomes
claims.note: Standard tax incidence: the tariff wedge lowers real purchasing power either through prices or through factor incomes.

claims.text: Heavy reliance on tariffs for government revenue makes an economy less efficient by misallocating resources
claims.note: Trade theory and cross-country experience show tariff-reliant economies protect low-productivity sectors; no rich country raises significant revenue from tariffs.

claims.text: Replacing income tax revenue with tariff revenue makes the federal tax system more regressive
claims.note: The US income tax is strongly progressive while a tariff burden is roughly proportional to consumption, so the swap shifts burden down the income scale.

claims.text: Inflation-indexed transfer programs blunt part of the tariff burden on the lowest-income households
claims.note: Social Security, SNAP and similar benefits adjust with the CPI, offsetting part of a tariff-driven price rise for recipients, with a lag.

claims.text: US shale producers are not boosting output in response to the oil spike because price volatility deters investment
claims.note: Dallas Fed surveys show executives prioritising capital discipline; drilling responds to sustained, not volatile, prices.

claims.text: Higher diesel, fertilizer and shipping costs from the oil shock pass through to consumer goods prices with a lag of months
claims.note: Energy and freight costs feed into food and goods prices over several months, as seen after the 2022 oil and fertilizer spike.

claims.text: Advanced economies are much less vulnerable to oil shocks than in the 1970s because oil intensity of GDP has fallen
claims.note: Oil use per unit of real GDP has fallen by well over half since 1973, so the same price shock has a smaller macro effect.

claims.text: The Iran conflict's energy shock has pushed US headline inflation higher [spring 2026]
claims.note: Headline CPI rose from 2.4% in February 2026 to 4.2% in May as the energy index went from +0.5% to +23.5% year over year and core stayed at 2.5-2.8%, so an energy shock did push headline inflation higher in spring 2026; the series do not themselves identify the Iran conflict as the cause.

claims.text: Higher oil prices do not benefit the US economy overall because consumer costs outweigh producer gains
claims.note: Since the shale boom the net GDP effect of oil shocks on the US is close to neutral, with producer gains roughly offsetting consumer losses, but the burden falls on households while gains accrue to a few states and firms.

claims.text: Pressuring gas station owners to cut prices does not materially lower pump prices
claims.note: Retail margins are a small, slow-moving part of the pump price, which tracks wholesale gasoline and crude.

claims.text: Renewable electricity does little to offset an oil supply shock because little oil is used for power generation
claims.note: Oil is a few percent of power generation in rich countries; its demand is in transport and petrochemicals, which electricity displaces only slowly through EVs.

claims.text: Oil prices will stay elevated for years after the Iran conflict ends because lost Gulf supply cannot be recovered
claims.note: Prediction; past Gulf disruptions saw prices normalise within a year or two, but this one has no precedent in scale.

claims.text: Tariffs have had only a modest effect on US inflation so far [mid-2025]
claims.note: The consumer price effect does not arrive at once: about half the direct effect is in place after three months and all of it by six, while the indirect effect more than doubles between six and twelve months, so by mid-2025 only part of the eventual effect (2.9 points on goods inflation by February 2026) had reached consumers.

claims.text: Tariffs have slowed US economic growth [2025]
claims.note: Forecasters cut 2025 growth after the tariffs and business investment weakened, but actual output held up better than expected, so the drag was real but modest.

claims.text: The 2025 tariffs weakened rather than strengthened the dollar because investors pulled back from US assets
claims.note: The dollar index fell roughly 10% in the first half of 2025 as foreign investors rotated out of US assets, the opposite of the textbook tariff effect.

claims.text: Tariff revenue is far too small to offset the deficit increase from the 2025 tax cuts
claims.note: CBO scored the 2025 tax law at over $3 trillion of added deficits against tariff revenue of a few hundred billion a year.

claims.text: Announced investment pledges overstate actual new investment because they include projects already planned
claims.note: Measured business fixed investment and foreign direct investment in 2025 ran near historical baselines, far below the pledged totals.

claims.text: Inflation was at a multi-decade high when the current administration took office [January 2025]
claims.note: The 12-month CPI change was 3.0% in January 2025, down from the 9.1% peak of June 2022 and below every reading from April 2021 to October 2023; the multi-decade high was in mid-2022, two and a half years earlier.

claims.text: Consumer prices overall are falling under the current administration [late 2025]
claims.note: The NSA CPI-U rose from 317.671 in January 2025 to 324.054 in December 2025 (+2.0%), with 12-month inflation of 2.7% in November and December 2025; the level was rising, not falling, even though December's unadjusted monthly change rounded to -0.0%.

claims.text: The US has no inflation [December 2025]
claims.note: CPI-U rose 2.7% in the 12 months to December 2025 (seasonally adjusted monthly change +0.3%), so the US had inflation of close to 3%, not none.

claims.text: Gasoline is cheaper now than it was under the previous administration [December 2025]
claims.note: December 2025 regular gasoline was 2.894, 16.4% below the Biden-period mean of 3.461 and 41.3% below the Biden peak of 4.929; only 3 of the 48 Biden months (Feb-Apr 2021: 2.501, 2.810, 2.858) were lower.

claims.text: The administration has secured well over ten trillion dollars of new investment in the US
claims.note: BEA recorded foreign direct investment of a few hundred billion in 2025 and trackers found roughly $600 billion of announced capital spending; the trillions are unverified pledges.

claims.text: The US is experiencing a manufacturing and factory-construction boom under the current administration
claims.note: Manufacturing employment fell through 2025-26 and manufacturing construction spending declined from its 2024 peak.

claims.text: Grocery prices are falling under the current administration [late 2025]
claims.note: The CPI food index rose from 335.517 in January 2025 to 343.795 in December 2025 (+2.5%), with 12-month food inflation of 3.1% in December 2025; the series covers all food (including food away from home) rather than groceries alone, hence the slightly lower confidence.

claims.text: Gasoline prices will fall once the administration's Iran policy succeeds
claims.note: Prediction conditional on an undefined success; pump prices track crude, which depends on when and how Hormuz traffic resumes.

claims.text: Strategic stock releases, bypass pipelines and Chinese import cuts kept the Hormuz closure from producing the feared oil price spike
claims.note: Coordinated IEA stock releases, Saudi and UAE pipeline bypasses and a sharp drop in Chinese crude imports replaced much of the lost flow; prices peaked far below the $150-200 bank forecasts.

claims.text: US strategic reserve releases and record exports cushioned Western fuel prices relative to Asia during the Hormuz closure
claims.note: US and Atlantic-basin supply is not routed through Hormuz, and SPR releases plus record exports added barrels, so Asian importers faced the tighter market.

claims.text: Bypass pipelines and alternative routes will permanently reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz
claims.note: Prediction; Gulf producers are expanding pipeline capacity but most Gulf export volume still has no alternative outlet.

claims.text: Tariffs reach consumer prices gradually over many months as pre-tariff inventory sells through and input costs propagate
claims.note: Pass-through arrives with a lag: the direct effect on imports is almost immediate but the domestic channels keep building for the better part of a year as higher input costs move through supply chains, with much of the adjustment at nine to twelve months; pre-tariff inventory is not examined.

claims.text: Tariffs pass through only partially to shelf prices because distribution margins make up a large share of what consumers pay
claims.note: A 1 percent rise in pre-retail prices raises consumer prices by 0.56 percent; since wholesale, retail and transportation margins are 53 percent of what consumers pay for tradable goods, complete cost pass-through implies a coefficient of about 0.47, which the estimate cannot be distinguished from.

claims.text: The effective tariff rate actually collected is well below the announced statutory rate because of exemptions and supplier switching
claims.note: The duty rate actually collected ran at roughly two-thirds of the statutory rate throughout, about 8.5 percent against 13 percent at the end of the sample, because of exemptions, exclusions, special entry, drawback and importers shifting away from the most heavily taxed sources.

claims.text: Tariffs are a very costly way to create jobs because consumer costs per job protected run far above wages
claims.note: Studies of the washing machine and steel tariffs put the consumer cost per job created in the hundreds of thousands of dollars a year.

claims.text: Tariffs persist for decades once imposed because protected industries lobby to keep them
claims.note: The 1964 truck tariff still stands and the 2018 tariffs were kept by the next administration; concentrated beneficiaries defend them.

claims.text: Tariffs on China pushed companies to diversify supply chains out of China
claims.note: After the 2018-2019 tariffs China's share of U.S. imports fell from nearly 25 percent to about 15 percent by 2024, and in 2025 it fell a further 5 points to below 10 percent, with Mexico and Vietnam gaining; the authors attribute the supply chain reorganisation to the higher tariff-inclusive import prices.

claims.text: Tariffs have not changed China's trade practices
claims.note: China did not meet its Phase One purchase commitments and expanded industrial subsidies and export volumes after 2018.

claims.text: Rising credit card debt alongside a low savings rate shows households are running out of money rather than spending from strength
claims.note: Record nominal card balances partly reflect population and price growth, but a falling savings rate and rising delinquencies do indicate strain rather than confident spending.

claims.text: Full Hormuz oil flows will take about a year to restore after the conflict
claims.note: Prediction; mine clearance, damaged facilities and insurer caution slow a restart, but the timeline depends on how the conflict ends.

claims.text: The US has no inflation [October 2026]
claims.note: The latest release (September 2026) shows CPI-U up 0.6% on the month and 3.7% over 12 months, the fastest 12-month pace since May 2026.

claims.text: Inflation is higher now than when the administration took office [October 2026]
claims.note: The 12-month CPI change was 3.0% in January 2025 and 3.7% in September 2026, the latest reading; core rose from 3.3% to 2.6% over the same span, so the increase is in headline inflation driven by energy.

claims.text: Tariffs added measurably to US consumer inflation over the year after they took effect
claims.note: By February 2026, a year after the tariffs began, they had added 2.9 percentage points to twelve-month consumer goods inflation in the sample, which would otherwise have been slightly negative; the sample excludes services, so the headline CPI contribution is smaller than the goods figure.

claims.text: The US economy is booming [2026]
claims.note: Real GDP grew at 2.5% and 2.2% annual rates in Q1 and Q2 2026, roughly trend growth, while payrolls averaged +45,000 a month and real hourly earnings fell 0.7% over the year; the economy is growing, but the data describe a solid expansion rather than a boom.

claims.text: US diesel prices reached record highs during the Iran conflict [spring 2026]
claims.note: Spring 2026 diesel peaked at 5.600 in May, below the prior record of 5.754 (Jun 2022); the series did set a record of 6.291 in Sep 2026, but not in spring.

claims.text: The rise in prices since 2025 is a direct result of the administration's policies
claims.note: Tariffs and the Iran war's oil shock are administration choices that raised prices, but part of the rise reflects global oil markets and pre-existing trends.

claims.text: Tariffs push prices up once, raising the price level, rather than causing ongoing inflation
claims.note: The tariff effect on the consumer goods price level peaked near 3 percent in February 2026 and stays positive, while the contribution to twelve-month goods inflation peaked at 2.9 points, falls to about zero by August 2026 and then turns negative as the 2025 increases drop out of the comparison.

claims.text: Without Fed accommodation, tariffs cause layoffs because nominal wages do not fall
claims.note: Downward nominal wage rigidity is well documented, so a real-income cut that is not absorbed by prices shows up in hiring and employment.

claims.text: Refunds of tariffs struck down by courts go to importers, not to the consumers who paid higher prices
claims.note: Customs refunds duties to the importer of record; there is no legal or practical channel to return them to retail buyers.

claims.text: A falling inflation rate means consumer prices are falling
claims.note: From January 2023 to September 2024 the 12-month inflation rate fell from 6.4% to 2.4% while the CPI-U level rose from 299.17 to 315.301; a falling rate means prices rise more slowly, not that they fall.

claims.text: Tariff pass-through studies cover only goods, a minority of consumer spending, so they cannot explain overall inflation
claims.note: The 67 CPI items in the study cover 75 percent of non-oil consumer goods spending but only 20 percent of the overall consumption basket, and the authors say their relative-price estimates are not a forecast of aggregate CPI inflation.

claims.text: Gains in the aggregate economy are accruing to the wealthy while lower-income households fall behind [2026]
claims.note: Spending and wealth gains have been concentrated in high-income households holding assets, while lower-income households report strain; the split is real but not a uniform decline for the lower 80%.

claims.text: High diesel prices are caused by Democratic environmental regulations
claims.note: Diesel sat at 3.49-3.82 through all of 2025 and Jan-Feb 2026 (below the 2022-2023 levels) under unchanged regulation, then jumped 32% in March 2026 (3.722 to 4.921) in the same month WTI rose 42%; the timing points to the oil shock, not to environmental rules that did not change that month.

claims.text: Core inflation is close to the Fed's target [autumn 2026]
claims.note: Core CPI rose 2.6% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 2.4% in August and 0.6 point above the 2% target (which is set on PCE inflation, usually a few tenths below CPI); the FOMC on September 16 still described inflation as elevated and raised rates.

claims.text: Higher long-term Treasury yields in 2026 mainly reflect stronger growth [2026]
claims.note: Growth is one driver, but the Fed chair also cites competition for capital and geopolitical commodity risk, and inflation above target lifts nominal yields too.

claims.text: Tariffs are driving a wave of domestic factory construction
claims.note: Some announced reshoring is real, but manufacturing employment fell in 2025 and tariff-exposed industries grew more slowly than lightly tariffed ones.

claims.text: The US economy is growing faster than any economy in history [2026]
claims.note: Real GDP grew at annual rates of 2.5% in Q1 and 2.2% in Q2 2026, ordinary trend-like growth, nowhere near a historical record.

claims.text: A bilateral trade deficit is money lost to the trading partner
claims.note: A trade deficit is goods received in exchange for payment, not a loss; economists do not treat bilateral deficits as transfers.

claims.text: US stock markets have set repeated record highs since the 2024 election [2026]
claims.note: Several autumn 2026 sources describe equities at or near record levels.

claims.text: Inflation has run above the Fed's target for more than five years [September 2026]
claims.note: The 12-month CPI-U change has been at least 2.3% in every month from March 2021 (2.6%) through September 2026 (3.7%), five and a half years; the Fed's target is on PCE inflation, which runs somewhat below CPI, so the lowest CPI readings (2.3% in April 2025) leave a small margin.

claims.text: Underlying inflation did not improve over the summer of 2026 [summer 2026]
claims.note: Core CPI 12-month growth fell from 2.8% in May 2026 to 2.6% in June, 2.5% in July and 2.4% in August before ticking back to 2.6% in September, and the June-August seasonally adjusted monthly readings (-0.0%, 0.2%, 0.3%) annualize to about 2%, so underlying inflation did improve over the summer before the September rebound.

claims.text: Monetary policy cannot offset an energy price spike but can stop it spreading into broader inflation
claims.note: Standard central-bank doctrine: rates act on demand and expectations, not oil supply, and second-round effects are what policy targets.

claims.text: The US labor market is at full employment [2026]
claims.note: Unemployment was 4.2% in September 2026 and has stayed in a 4.1-4.3% range since March, near common estimates of the natural rate, but payroll growth was weak (+29,000, 45,000/month average) and the release does not define full employment.

claims.text: Inflation hurts households without financial assets the most
claims.note: Paycheck-to-paycheck households cannot offset price rises with asset gains and spend more of their income on energy and food.

claims.text: Inflation pressures in 2026 are global rather than specific to the US [2026]
claims.note: The 2026 oil shock hit every importer and the ECB also hiked twice, though US tariffs are a US-specific source.

claims.text: Inflation can be returned to target without raising unemployment [2026]
claims.note: A forecast; the 2022-24 disinflation happened without recession, but tightening into a supply shock has often cost jobs.

claims.text: Tariff costs are absorbed in importer and exporter margins rather than passed to consumers
claims.note: Border pass-through is about 90 percent, so exporters absorb little; domestic producers pass input tariffs into producer prices; and a 10 percent rise in tariff-induced pre-retail prices raises retail prices 5.6 percent, consistent with complete pass-through net of distribution margins rather than absorption in margins.

claims.text: Firms cannot pass tariffs on because consumers are too stretched to accept higher prices
claims.note: Regional business surveys found most tariff-paying firms had already passed at least some of the cost on through higher prices, and nearly half still planned further tariff-induced increases a year on.

claims.text: Tariffs do not slow economic growth
claims.note: Most estimates put the 2025 tariffs at a drag of roughly half a point of GDP; no recession followed but growth was lower than otherwise.

claims.text: Tariffs cut the trade deficit and boosted GDP [spring 2025]
claims.note: Imports fell in Q2 2025 after Q1 front-running, lifting measured GDP that quarter, but the 2025 goods deficit ended about equal to 2024.

claims.text: Economists' warnings that tariffs would tank the economy proved wrong [2025]
claims.note: No recession occurred in 2025, but prices rose and growth slowed; most mainstream forecasts predicted a drag, not a collapse.

claims.text: Government debt is sustainable when nominal GDP grows faster than the debt
claims.note: Debt dynamics depend on the gap between nominal growth and the deficit plus interest; this is standard public finance.

claims.text: Inflation is low by historical standards [January 2026]
claims.note: Headline CPI was 2.4% in January 2026, tied for the lowest reading since February 2021 (2.3% in April 2025), far below the 9.1% peak of June 2022 and about the 2019-20 pre-pandemic pace (2.3-2.5%); it remained above the 2% target, and the series only spans 2019-2026.

claims.text: Real wages rose over the past year as pay outpaced inflation [January 2026]
claims.note: Derived real average hourly earnings rose 1.2% in the 12 months to January 2026 (nominal AHE +3.7% vs CPI +2.4%).

claims.text: Real wages never grew in any year of the Biden administration
claims.note: Derived real average hourly earnings growth was positive every month from May 2023 through January 2025, including +0.8% in December 2023 and +1.2% in December 2024, so real wages grew in 2023 and 2024 after falling in 2021-22.

claims.text: Inflation fell in the year after the 2025 tariffs were imposed [January 2026]
claims.note: Headline CPI fell from 3.0% in January 2025 (2.8% in February) to 2.4% in January 2026 and core from 3.3% to 2.5%, though headline dipped to 2.3% in April 2025 and rebounded to 3.0% by September 2025 before easing; the series settle the direction of the rate, not any causal role of tariffs.

claims.text: Consumer prices only fall outright during a recession or depression
claims.note: Single-month declines in the all-items index occur outside recessions (seasonally adjusted -0.4% in June 2026; unadjusted declines in late 2022 and late 2023), but in 2019-2026 the 12-month change never went negative, not even in the 2020 recession (low of 0.1% in May 2020), so sustained outright deflation did not occur in any condition covered.

claims.text: Gasoline and egg prices are down under the current administration [early 2026]
claims.note: The gasoline half holds for early 2026: Jan and Feb 2026 regular gasoline (2.809, 2.908) were 8.7% and 5.5% below the January 2025 inauguration-month price of 3.076, though the gap vanished in March 2026 (3.638); the egg half is outside this series.

claims.text: There has been no inflation under the current administration [2025]
claims.note: The 12-month CPI-U change ran between 2.3% and 3.0% in every month of 2025, and the index rose 2.0% from January to December 2025.

claims.text: Grocery and housing prices remain high even as the inflation rate has fallen [late 2025]
claims.note: By December 2025 the shelter index was 420.134, 28% above December 2020 (327.702) and still rising 3.2% a year, and the food index was 343.795, 27% above December 2020 (270.023), while headline inflation had fallen to 2.7%; falling inflation left price levels elevated.

claims.text: Removing the tariffs would be good for the US economy
claims.note: Most models find the 2025 tariffs a net drag on output and real incomes, so removing them raises GDP modestly.

claims.text: Cooling inflation in late 2025 reflected a slowing economy rather than policy success [late 2025]
claims.note: Unemployment drifted up to about 4.6% and oil fell in 2025, both disinflationary, alongside the fading of the 2021-22 shock.

claims.text: Tariff revenue is small relative to federal interest costs and the deficit
claims.note: Tariffs raised roughly $200-300 billion a year against about $1.2 trillion of interest and a near-$2 trillion deficit.

claims.text: Consumer sentiment about current conditions hit a record low [December 2025]
claims.note: The University of Michigan current-conditions index set a record low in December 2025 even as expectations improved.

claims.text: Inflation over the most recent three months has run below the Fed's two percent target [October 2026]
claims.note: Seasonally adjusted CPI-U rose from 332.568 in June to 336.298 in September 2026 (+1.1% in three months, about 4.6% annualized), far above 2%; the claim held only for the June-August window (May 333.979 to August 334.131, about 0.2% annualized) because of June's energy-driven -0.4% month.

claims.text: Shelter costs are still rising faster than overall core inflation [September 2026]
claims.note: Shelter rose 3.2% over the 12 months to September 2026 versus 2.6% for all items less food and energy, and 0.4% versus 0.3% on the month.

claims.text: Cumulative price increases under the current administration are far smaller than under the previous one [2026]
claims.note: CPI-U rose 21.4% from January 2021 to January 2025 (261.582 to 317.671) and 6.1% from January 2025 to September 2026 (to 336.94); the cumulative figure is far smaller, but it covers 20 months versus 48, and annualized the pace is 3.6% versus 5.0%, a smaller gap.

claims.text: Annual inflation under the previous administration peaked near twenty percent
claims.note: The 12-month CPI-U change peaked at 9.1% in June 2022; no month in 2021-2024 exceeded that, and nothing approached twenty percent.

claims.text: Producer prices are rising faster than consumer prices, pointing to further consumer inflation [autumn 2026]
claims.note: PPI rose 1.3% in September 2026, over 6% year on year, but producer prices pass through to CPI only partially and with lags.

claims.text: Tariffs have not reduced the overall US trade deficit [2025]
claims.note: The 2025 goods deficit was roughly unchanged at about $1.2 trillion as trade shifted from China to Mexico and Asia.

claims.text: Tariffs shifted US imports away from China rather than cutting imports overall
claims.note: China's share of U.S. non-oil imports fell another 5 points to below 10 percent in January-November 2025 while Mexico and Vietnam gained the most share; the post documents the shift but says nothing about whether total imports fell.

claims.text: Tariffs have not revived US manufacturing employment [2025]
claims.note: Manufacturing employment hit a recent low in December 2025 according to BLS, so it declined over 2025; the 72,000 recovery since then is a 2026 development and the release says nothing about tariffs as the cause.

claims.text: Industries facing higher tariffs grew more slowly than lightly tariffed ones [2025]
claims.note: Industrial production split by tariff exposure showed autos and metals lagging pharma and electronics in 2025.

claims.text: Most lost US manufacturing jobs are due to technology, not trade
claims.note: Automation explains most of the long-run decline, but China-shock studies attribute a substantial share of 2000s losses to trade.

claims.text: Most consumer prices are falling [October 2026]
claims.note: In September 2026 the all-items index rose 0.6% and core 0.3%, with recreation, used cars, education, airline fares, medical care and apparel all up; BLS says communication was among the small number of major indexes that decreased.

claims.text: Average consumer prices are lower than when the current administration took office [October 2026]
claims.note: The NSA CPI-U rose from 317.671 in January 2025 to 336.94 in September 2026, a 6.1% increase in the average price level.

claims.text: Inflation has stayed above three percent since the Iran war began [October 2026]
claims.note: Headline 12-month CPI was 3.3% in March 2026, 3.8% April, 4.2% May, 3.5% June, 3.4% July, 3.4% August and 3.7% September, every month since the March 2026 gasoline jump (+24.9%) that marks the conflict's onset in the price data; the war's start date itself is not in these documents.

claims.text: Iran effectively controls the Strait of Hormuz despite the declared end of the war [autumn 2026]
claims.note: Depends on shipping data; a CNBC traffic analysis showed a three-month low in transits while the administration claims total control.

claims.text: Oil prices are being held below fundamentals by strategic reserve releases and political headlines [autumn 2026]
claims.note: A market call; reserve draws do add temporary supply, but whether the price is wrong cannot be settled from the data cited.

claims.text: Gasoline prices are high relative to the current crude oil price [autumn 2026]
claims.note: Regular gasoline minus the crude cost per gallon (WTI/42) was 2.04 in Sep 2026 (4.355 minus 97.31/42) and about 2.02-2.06 every month since June 2026, against 1.54-1.71 in Sep 2023, Sep 2024 and Sep 2025 and 2.20 at the Jun 2022 peak, so the retail margin over crude is roughly 0.35-0.50 per gallon above its recent norm; October crude is not yet in the file.

claims.text: A return to war with Iran would raise US consumer prices sharply [autumn 2026]
claims.note: A conditional forecast about a renewed conflict.

claims.text: The US strategic petroleum reserve is too depleted to keep offsetting supply losses [autumn 2026]
claims.note: The SPR fell below 300 million barrels, its lowest since the 1980s, which constrains but does not end releases.

claims.text: Inflation rose after the 2025 tariffs took effect [2026]
claims.note: Headline CPI rose from 2.3% in April 2025 to 3.0% by September 2025 and 3.7% by September 2026, and core goods went from -0.1% (March 2025) to +1.5% (September 2025); but core CPI is lower now (2.6%) than when the tariffs took effect (2.8%) and the 2026 headline rise is energy-driven, so the rise is real but mostly not in the categories tariffs touch.

claims.text: The US economy is resilient with no recession in sight [early 2026]
claims.note: Real GDP grew 2.5% annualized in Q1 2026 and 2.2% in Q2, with consumer spending, investment and exports contributing, and unemployment stayed at 4.3-4.4% in early 2026; no contraction appears in the data for the period.

claims.text: Recent job gains are concentrated in health care, signalling underlying weakness [early 2026]
claims.note: Over the 12 months to September 2026 health care added an average 33,000 jobs a month against 45,000 for total nonfarm payrolls, about three quarters of all gains, with employment in all other major industries little changed; the release measures the concentration, and the 'weakness' reading is the claim's interpretation of that narrow base.

claims.text: Interest rates are stable and likely to fall [early 2026]
claims.note: On September 16, 2026 the FOMC raised the federal funds target range by a quarter point to 3.75-4%, the opposite of the predicted fall; the statement does not show the early-2026 rate path, so this only settles the prediction's outcome.

claims.text: The new Fed chair is a hawk who wants to cut rates aggressively
claims.note: A hawk favours higher rates to fight inflation; Warsh went on to raise rates in September 2026.

claims.text: Energy prices will fall rapidly once the Iran war ends [October 2026]
claims.note: A prediction; a quick fall depends on Gulf shipping reopening and refined-product supply recovering.

claims.text: Oil is cheaper now than it was under the previous administration [October 2026]
claims.note: WTI averaged 97.31 in Sep 2026 (latest month), 22% above the Biden-period (Feb 2021-Jan 2025) mean of 79.74 and 15% below the Biden peak of 114.84 (Jun 2022); only 5 of the 48 Biden months (Mar-Jul 2022) were higher than Sep 2026, so oil is dearer than under the typical Biden-era month.

claims.text: Inflation is about to overtake wage growth, cutting real purchasing power [spring 2026]
claims.note: Derived real average hourly earnings growth went from +1.2% in February 2026 to +0.1% in March, -0.2% in April and -0.8% in May as CPI inflation (3.3%, 3.8%, 4.2%) overtook nominal wage growth (3.4%, 3.6%, 3.3%).

claims.text: When inflation outruns wages, workers demand raises that push prices up further in a wage-price spiral
claims.note: The mechanism exists, but post-2021 evidence shows spirals are rare when expectations stay anchored and labor bargaining power is weak.

claims.text: Households are taking on more debt to maintain living standards as prices outpace pay [2026]
claims.note: Card balances and delinquencies rose in 2025-26, though rising balances partly reflect nominal growth rather than distress.

claims.text: Credit card default rates have reached 2008 levels [2026]
claims.note: Card charge-off rates in 2025-26 approached 2008 levels but stayed below the 2009-10 peak above 10%.

claims.text: Moderate inflation is harmless if wages keep pace
claims.note: Real incomes determine living standards; 2% targets reflect that moderate, anticipated inflation has small costs.

claims.text: The first-term tariffs raised large revenue without raising inflation [2018-2020]
claims.note: Inflation stayed near 2% in 2018-19, but tariffed goods such as washing machines rose in price and total first-term tariff revenue was roughly $230 billion, paid by US importers.

claims.text: Tariffs cause only temporary short-term disruption
claims.note: The tariff contribution to twelve-month goods inflation is temporary, fading to zero within about eighteen months, but tariffs leave the consumer goods price level permanently higher and the full effect takes a year to appear; the post covers prices only, not wider economic effects.

claims.text: Other countries charge the US tariffs while the US charges them none
claims.note: The US applied tariffs averaging about 3% before 2025 with high peaks on trucks, footwear and sugar; most partners' averages were similar.

claims.text: The EU's VAT acts like a tariff on US exports
claims.note: VAT applies equally to domestic and imported goods and is rebated on exports, so it does not discriminate against US products.

claims.text: The three-month annualized inflation rate is too volatile to guide policy
claims.note: Shifting the window by one month moves the three-month annualized CPI rate from about 0.2% (June-August 2026, after June's -0.4%) to about 4.6% (July-September 2026), demonstrating the volatility; whether that makes it unfit to guide policy is a judgment the data do not settle.

claims.text: Trade partners will keep their tariff deals despite the Supreme Court ruling [2026]
claims.note: Many partners signalled they would keep their deals, but the EU froze implementation of its side after the ruling.

claims.text: Tariffs could replace the federal income tax
claims.note: Tariffs raise roughly $200-300 billion a year against about $2.5 trillion of individual income tax; imports are too small a base.

claims.text: Grocery prices are down under the current administration [2025]
claims.note: The CPI food index rose 2.5% from January to December 2025 (335.517 to 343.795) and was up 3.1% year over year in December 2025; the series covers all food including restaurants rather than groceries alone.

claims.text: Gasoline is cheaper now than it was under the previous administration [2025]
claims.note: Regular gasoline averaged 3.101 over Feb-Dec 2025 (range 2.894-3.171), 10.4% below the Biden-period mean of 3.461 and 37% below the Biden peak of 4.929, with every 2025 month under the Biden mean; the caveat is that 2025 was essentially flat against the final Biden months (Oct 2024-Jan 2025: 3.137, 3.053, 3.018, 3.076), so the gap is against the Biden average, not the handover price.

claims.text: Energy prices are down overall under the current administration [2025]
claims.note: The energy index was below its year-earlier level from February through July 2025 (-0.2% to -3.7%) but turned positive from August, ending 2025 at 274.131, 0.4% above January 2025 (273.045) and 2.3% above December 2024; down for much of the year, not down overall by year end.

claims.text: Electricity prices are rising even as fuel prices fall [2025]
claims.note: Retail electricity rose roughly 5-6% in 2025 on data-center demand and grid costs.

claims.text: Beef prices are rising sharply [2025]
claims.note: Ground beef hit record highs in 2025 on the smallest US cattle herd in decades.

claims.text: Wage averages hide that low-income workers fare worse during inflation
claims.note: In 2021-24 low-wage workers saw the fastest real gains; in 2026 production workers' real pay fell slightly more than the average.

claims.text: Moderating gasoline prices quickly lift real wages
claims.note: In June 2026 the seasonally adjusted gasoline index fell 9.7%, pulling all-items CPI down 0.4% while nominal AHE rose 0.3%, and derived real hourly earnings jumped 0.7% in the month (11.225 to 11.303), reversing most of the spring's loss; one episode, but it shows the mechanism.

claims.text: Tariffs and energy shocks that keep inflation elevated push long-term Treasury yields and mortgage rates higher
claims.note: Nominal long yields embed expected inflation, so policies that raise expected inflation raise borrowing costs, though how much of the 2026 yield rise is tariff-driven is contested.

claims.text: Tariffs, immigration restrictions and the Iran war are each adding to US inflation [2026]
claims.note: Tariff pass-through and the war-driven energy spike are well documented; the labor-supply effect of immigration curbs on prices is real but smaller and harder to measure.

claims.text: The CPI is an accurate measure of the change in the typical household's cost of living
claims.note: The CPI is the consensus measure built from hundreds of thousands of price quotes; known biases are small relative to the gap between measured and perceived inflation.

claims.text: The CPI methodology has not been changed to lower measured inflation [2026]
claims.note: The 2026 methodological tweaks were to the BEA's PCE deflator, scheduled in advance; the BLS CPI series was unchanged.

claims.text: Perceived inflation runs above measured inflation because people weight salient prices like gasoline and remember losses more than gains
claims.note: Survey research consistently finds inflation perceptions track gasoline and grocery prices and show loss aversion and telescoping bias.

claims.text: Rising producer input costs eventually pass through into consumer prices
claims.note: A 10 percent duty on imported inputs raises producer prices in consumer goods industries by about 2.6 percent, and a 10 percent tariff-induced rise in pre-retail prices raises retail prices by 5.6 percent, consistent with full pass-through net of distribution margins, with the input-cost channel taking nine to twelve months.

claims.text: Tariffs raised US inflation by a modest amount spread over time rather than causing a surge
claims.note: Only about a quarter of a tariff reaches consumer goods prices, and the indirect channels build slowly, with marginal cost pass-through becoming significant only at nine to twelve months, so the full effect arrives over about a year rather than as a surge.

claims.text: The US economy's low import share limits how much tariffs raise its overall price level
claims.note: The direct effect scales with the imported share of each good and a uniform 10 percent tariff raises consumer goods prices only 2.6 percent, but a third of that effect comes through domestically produced goods via imported inputs and markups, so a low import share limits the effect less than the direct channel alone would suggest.

claims.text: On-again, off-again tariff implementation slowed how fast firms passed tariffs into prices
claims.note: Retail pass-through in 2025 was gradual and incomplete, consistent with firms waiting, but price trackers also saw some sellers raise prices as soon as tariffs were announced.

claims.text: Tariffs lower real wages because they raise prices without raising the revenue firms could use for pay rises
claims.note: Tariffs do reduce real incomes as a cost-push shock, but protected domestic producers gain revenue and nominal wages are not literally frozen.

claims.text: Consumer spending has stayed strong despite tariffs, higher gas prices and policy uncertainty [2026]
claims.note: The FOMC's September 16, 2026 statement says domestic spending has been resilient despite elevated geopolitical uncertainty, and BEA lists consumer spending as a contributor to Q2 2026 GDP growth; neither document quantifies spending growth.

claims.text: Households have sustained spending through higher gas prices by cutting their savings rate rather than other purchases [2026]
claims.note: The personal saving rate fell by about two points over the year while real spending held up, which is consistent with dissaving to absorb fuel costs.

claims.text: Underlying inflation is running around three percent and not decelerating [2026]
claims.note: Core CPI ran 2.4-2.9% through 2026 (2.6% in September) and core services 2.9-3.4%, so 'around three' overstates core slightly; and it did decelerate, from 3.0-3.1% in mid-2025 to 2.4% in August 2026, before rebounding to 2.6%.

claims.text: Underlying inflation is returning to the Fed's target and was only temporarily lifted by tariffs and the Iran war [2026]
claims.note: Tariff and energy effects are expected to fade, but core measures stayed near three percent through 2026 with services inflation showing no clear downtrend.

claims.text: Public anger over prices reflects the cumulative price level since 2021, not just the current inflation rate
claims.note: Consumer sentiment stayed depressed even as inflation slowed in 2023-24, tracking the roughly quarter rise in the price level since 2020.

claims.text: Returning prices to pre-2021 levels would require a deflationary collapse in demand and mass unemployment
claims.note: Broad price declines of twenty percent or more have historically occurred only in severe depressions.

claims.text: Tariff costs have led US businesses to hold back on hiring
claims.note: Business surveys report tariff-related hiring restraint and manufacturing payrolls fell, but overall unemployment stayed near four percent.

claims.text: Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries are a major cause of high US diesel prices [autumn 2026]
claims.note: Russia was the second-largest diesel exporter and its export ban after refinery strikes tightened global supply, but the Iran war and Gulf disruption are the larger factor.

claims.text: Importing a few million barrels of Russian diesel is too small to materially lower US diesel prices
claims.note: US distillate consumption is around four million barrels a day, so a one-off shipment of a few million barrels is a rounding error in a global market.

claims.text: Short of ending the Iran war, the administration has few tools to lower diesel prices quickly
claims.note: Export bans and reserve releases give only brief relief in a globally priced fuel market; the supply disruption itself sets the price.

claims.text: Gasoline prices are the main driver of the recent rise in headline inflation [spring 2026]
claims.note: In March 2026 the seasonally adjusted gasoline index rose 21.2% and energy 10.9% while all items rose 0.9% and core only 0.2%; headline 12-month inflation jumped from 2.4% to 3.3% that month while core moved from 2.5% to 2.6%, so gasoline accounts for essentially all of the spring rise.

claims.text: Prices raised by a tariff do not fall back when the tariff is removed
claims.note: Prices fall more slowly than they rise, but when the washing-machine tariff actually ended in 2023 laundry prices dropped about a tenth within a year.

claims.text: Tariffs hit low-margin cheap goods hardest, so they fall disproportionately on lower-income shoppers
claims.note: Tariffs are regressive because lower-income households spend a larger share on tradable goods and discount sellers have no margin to absorb duties.

claims.text: Monetary policy cannot offset the price effects of a tariff supply shock
claims.note: Rates cannot lower import costs, but they can restrain second-round price effects, which is why the Fed treats tariff inflation as a judgment call rather than untouchable.

claims.text: Removing tariffs lowers prices only gradually, as imposing them raised prices gradually
claims.note: Prices do adjust downward with a lag when tariffs truly end, but the asymmetry is larger than symmetric: price cuts come slower and smaller than the rises.

claims.text: Manufacturing employment fell during the first year of the new tariffs [2025]
claims.note: BLS describes December 2025 as a recent low for manufacturing employment (up 72,000 since), which means the sector shed jobs through 2025, though the release does not give the January-December 2025 change.

claims.text: Overall consumer prices will fall under the administration's policies
claims.note: The CPI has risen about three to four percent a year through 2026; broad price declines occur only in deep recessions.

claims.text: AI data-center demand is pushing up electricity and computer prices [2026]
claims.note: Data-center load is raising wholesale power demand and memory chip shortages lifted computer prices, but fuel costs and grid investment also drive electricity bills.

claims.text: Grocery inflation has slowed sharply [September 2026]
claims.note: Food at home rose 1.8% over the 12 months to September 2026 with monthly changes of -0.1%, 0.0% and -0.1% in July-September, and the broader food index slowed from 3.2% (April 2026) to 2.5%; beef fell 1.0% and dairy 0.9% on the month.

claims.text: Core inflation fell to its lowest level in more than five years [late 2025]
claims.note: Core CPI was 2.6% in November and December 2025, the lowest since March 2021 (1.6%), which is four years and eight months, not more than five years; April 2021 was already 3.0%.

claims.text: Gasoline is cheaper now than it was under the previous administration [early 2026]
claims.note: January and February 2026 regular gasoline were 2.809 and 2.908 (mean 2.859), 17.4% below the Biden-period mean of 3.461 and 42% below the 4.929 peak; it stopped being true in the second week of March 2026 (weekly 03/09 3.502) and March's monthly average of 3.638 was already above the Biden mean.

claims.text: Prices of groceries, rent, hotels and cars are lower than when the administration took office [early 2026]
claims.note: The food index rose 2.9% from January 2025 to January 2026 (335.517 to 345.165) and shelter rose 3.0% (409.153 to 421.526), so groceries and rent were higher, not lower; hotels and cars are not in these series.

claims.text: Mortgage rates are at their lowest in four years and falling [early 2026]
claims.note: Thirty-year rates near six percent in early 2026 were the lowest since 2022 but above early-2022 levels, and they rose back above seven percent later in the year.

claims.text: Gasoline prices mainly follow the global oil market rather than presidential policy
claims.note: Pump prices tracked crude under both administrations: WTI 91.64 to 114.84 (Feb-Jun 2022) with gasoline 3.517 to 4.929, WTI 64.51 to 102.13 (Feb-May 2026) with gasoline 2.908 to 4.479, and the 2025 decline of WTI to 57.97 with gasoline easing to 2.894; co-movement supports the claim but cannot exclude policy effects on crude itself.

claims.text: A US diesel export ban would lower prices only briefly before refiners cut output and global prices rise
claims.note: Energy economists across the spectrum reached the same conclusion on 2022 export-ban proposals: trapped supply lowers Gulf Coast prices for weeks, then refinery cuts and higher world prices reverse it.

claims.text: Tariffs have hurt farmers by lowering crop prices and raising fertilizer costs
claims.note: Chinese retaliation collapsed US soybean exports in 2025 and tariffs on imported fertilizer raised input costs, both documented in USDA data.

claims.text: Retailers raise prices as soon as a tariff is announced, pricing the next shipment rather than past costs
claims.note: Retailers take a few months to pass on higher costs: only about half of the direct effect of a tariff is in consumer prices after three months and all of it by six, so retail prices do not jump at announcement.

claims.text: Refunding past tariffs does not lower prices while replacement tariffs keep restocking costs high
claims.note: Prices track replacement cost; a refund of sunk duties is a windfall to the balance sheet while new tariffs keep the marginal import cost elevated.

claims.text: Tariff revenue is little changed by the Supreme Court ruling because replacement tariffs collect similar amounts [2026]
claims.note: Monthly customs receipts after the ruling stayed several times their 2024 level as Section 122 and 232 tariffs replaced the emergency ones, though below the 2025 peak.

claims.text: Raising the policy rate brings inflation back toward target sooner
claims.note: Tighter policy restrains demand and anchors expectations, lowering inflation with a lag of a year or more; it cannot undo a supply shock already in prices.

claims.text: Tariffs invite retaliatory tariffs from trading partners
claims.note: Every major US tariff round since 2018 drew matching retaliation from China, the EU, Canada and others.

claims.text: Lower-income households are relying on credit and missing payments as prices outrun pay [2026]
claims.note: Credit card and auto delinquency rates rose through 2025-26, concentrated among lower-income and younger borrowers.

claims.text: Current inflation is a temporary by-product of the Iran war that will reverse when the war ends [spring 2026]
claims.note: The energy component should reverse when supply normalizes, but core inflation near three percent and tariff pass-through are not war-related and will not vanish with a ceasefire.

claims.text: US seizures of Iranian oil cargoes are holding down world oil prices [spring 2026]
claims.note: No independent accounting of seized or released volumes exists; oil near eighty-five dollars mostly reflects spare OPEC capacity and demand rather than seizures.

claims.text: Oil prices have stayed well below the worst-case forecasts made when the Iran war began [spring 2026]
claims.note: Some analysts warned a Hormuz closure could push crude past one hundred fifty dollars; prices in the eighties to low hundreds were well short of that.

claims.text: Non-emergency Section 232 and 301 tariffs raised about as much revenue as the emergency tariffs [2025]
claims.note: Trade economists estimated the emergency tariffs accounted for roughly two-thirds of 2025 collections, well above the Section 232 and 301 take.

claims.text: Refunds of the struck-down emergency tariffs will be delayed by years of litigation
claims.note: Customs certified and paid out most of the refunds within months of the ruling.

claims.text: Replacement legal authorities let the administration keep a global tariff in place despite the ruling [2026]
claims.note: After the Supreme Court ruled in February 2026 that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs, the fentanyl and reciprocal tariffs were terminated and replaced with a temporary 10 percent surcharge on all imports under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, while Section 232 product tariffs continued.

claims.text: Gasoline prices rise seasonally into the summer driving months
claims.note: Prices do rise from winter toward summer (May above January in 15 of 16 years 2010-2025), but the seasonal peak is typically late spring, not midsummer: May was at or above August in 13 of those 16 years (2024: May 3.603, Aug 3.389; 2019: 2.859 vs 2.621), so prices usually plateau or drift down during the driving season itself.
