thinEvidence.note: DRAM and NAND contract prices rose sharply from late 2025 on AI data-center demand, lifting PC and phone prices.

thinEvidence.text: Moderate inflation is harmless if wages keep pace
thinEvidence.note: Real incomes determine living standards; 2% targets reflect that moderate, anticipated inflation has small costs.

thinEvidence.text: Monetary policy cannot offset an energy price spike but can stop it spreading into broader inflation
thinEvidence.note: Standard central-bank doctrine: rates act on demand and expectations, not oil supply, and second-round effects are what policy targets.

thinEvidence.text: Monetary policy cannot offset the price effects of a tariff supply shock
thinEvidence.note: Rates cannot lower import costs, but they can restrain second-round price effects, which is why the Fed treats tariff inflation as a judgment call rather than untouchable.

thinEvidence.text: Monetary tightening does little to curb inflation caused by an oil supply shock
thinEvidence.note: Rate hikes work on demand and cannot add oil supply, though they can anchor expectations and limit second-round effects, as the Fed argued in 2022.

thinEvidence.text: Mortgage rates are at their lowest in four years and falling [early 2026]
thinEvidence.note: Thirty-year rates near six percent in early 2026 were the lowest since 2022 but above early-2022 levels, and they rose back above seven percent later in the year.

thinEvidence.text: Most academic economists hold that tariffs leave the average American worse off
thinEvidence.note: IGM Forum panels in 2018 and 2024 showed large majorities disagreeing that tariffs improve Americans' welfare.

thinEvidence.text: Most lost US manufacturing jobs are due to technology, not trade
thinEvidence.note: Automation explains most of the long-run decline, but China-shock studies attribute a substantial share of 2000s losses to trade.

thinEvidence.text: The new Fed chair is a hawk who wants to cut rates aggressively
thinEvidence.note: A hawk favours higher rates to fight inflation; Warsh went on to raise rates in September 2026.

thinEvidence.text: Non-emergency Section 232 and 301 tariffs raised about as much revenue as the emergency tariffs [2025]
thinEvidence.note: Trade economists estimated the emergency tariffs accounted for roughly two-thirds of 2025 collections, well above the Section 232 and 301 take.

thinEvidence.text: Oil prices have stayed well below the worst-case forecasts made when the Iran war began [spring 2026]
thinEvidence.note: Some analysts warned a Hormuz closure could push crude past one hundred fifty dollars; prices in the eighties to low hundreds were well short of that.

thinEvidence.text: Oil prices are being held below fundamentals by strategic reserve releases and political headlines [autumn 2026]
thinEvidence.note: A market call; reserve draws do add temporary supply, but whether the price is wrong cannot be settled from the data cited.

thinEvidence.text: Oil prices will stay elevated for years after the Iran conflict ends because lost Gulf supply cannot be recovered
thinEvidence.note: Prediction; past Gulf disruptions saw prices normalise within a year or two, but this one has no precedent in scale.

thinEvidence.text: Over recent decades US real hourly pay has grown only slowly, with frequent down years
thinEvidence.note: BLS production-worker earnings deflated by CPI rose about 23 percent from 1990 to 2026, about 0.6 percent a year, with a third of years negative.

thinEvidence.text: Overall consumer prices will fall under the administration's policies
thinEvidence.note: The CPI has risen about three to four percent a year through 2026; broad price declines occur only in deep recessions.

thinEvidence.text: Owners' equivalent rent measures a housing cost that no one actually pays
thinEvidence.note: OER is imputed rather than paid in cash, but it is the standard way to measure the consumption value of owner-occupied housing and tracks market rents with a lag.

thinEvidence.text: Perceived inflation runs above measured inflation because people weight salient prices like gasoline and remember losses more than gains
thinEvidence.note: Survey research consistently finds inflation perceptions track gasoline and grocery prices and show loss aversion and telescoping bias.

thinEvidence.text: Pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz cushion the loss of supply when the strait closes
thinEvidence.note: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline (about 5 million barrels a day to Yanbu) and the UAE's Habshan-Fujairah line can carry a large share of Gulf exports around the strait.

thinEvidence.text: Pressuring gas station owners to cut prices does not materially lower pump prices
thinEvidence.note: Retail margins are a small, slow-moving part of the pump price, which tracks wholesale gasoline and crude.

thinEvidence.text: Public anger over prices reflects the cumulative price level since 2021, not just the current inflation rate
thinEvidence.note: Consumer sentiment stayed depressed even as inflation slowed in 2023-24, tracking the roughly quarter rise in the price level since 2020.

thinEvidence.text: Refunding past tariffs does not lower prices while replacement tariffs keep restocking costs high
thinEvidence.note: Prices track replacement cost; a refund of sunk duties is a windfall to the balance sheet while new tariffs keep the marginal import cost elevated.

thinEvidence.text: Refunds of the struck-down emergency tariffs will be delayed by years of litigation
thinEvidence.note: Customs certified and paid out most of the refunds within months of the ruling.

thinEvidence.text: Refunds of tariffs struck down by courts go to importers, not to the consumers who paid higher prices
thinEvidence.note: Customs refunds duties to the importer of record; there is no legal or practical channel to return them to retail buyers.

thinEvidence.text: Removing the tariffs would be good for the US economy
thinEvidence.note: Most models find the 2025 tariffs a net drag on output and real incomes, so removing them raises GDP modestly.

thinEvidence.text: Replacing income tax revenue with tariff revenue makes the federal tax system more regressive
thinEvidence.note: The US income tax is strongly progressive while a tariff burden is roughly proportional to consumption, so the swap shifts burden down the income scale.

thinEvidence.text: Retaliation against US tariffs cut farm exports enough to require federal bailouts of farmers
thinEvidence.note: China's retaliatory tariffs cut US soybean exports sharply in 2018 and the USDA paid about 23 billion dollars in Market Facilitation Program aid in 2018-2019.

thinEvidence.text: A return to war with Iran would raise US consumer prices sharply [autumn 2026]
thinEvidence.note: A conditional forecast about a renewed conflict.

thinEvidence.text: Returning prices to pre-2021 levels would require a deflationary collapse in demand and mass unemployment
thinEvidence.note: Broad price declines of twenty percent or more have historically occurred only in severe depressions.

thinEvidence.text: The rise in prices since 2025 is a direct result of the administration's policies
thinEvidence.note: Tariffs and the Iran war's oil shock are administration choices that raised prices, but part of the rise reflects global oil markets and pre-existing trends.

thinEvidence.text: Rising credit card debt alongside a low savings rate shows households are running out of money rather than spending from strength
thinEvidence.note: Record nominal card balances partly reflect population and price growth, but a falling savings rate and rising delinquencies do indicate strain rather than confident spending.

thinEvidence.text: US seizures of Iranian oil cargoes are holding down world oil prices [spring 2026]
thinEvidence.note: No independent accounting of seized or released volumes exists; oil near eighty-five dollars mostly reflects spare OPEC capacity and demand rather than seizures.

thinEvidence.text: US shale producers are not boosting output in response to the oil spike because price volatility deters investment
thinEvidence.note: Dallas Fed surveys show executives prioritising capital discipline; drilling responds to sustained, not volatile, prices.

thinEvidence.text: Short of ending the Iran war, the administration has few tools to lower diesel prices quickly
thinEvidence.note: Export bans and reserve releases give only brief relief in a globally priced fuel market; the supply disruption itself sets the price.

thinEvidence.text: Short-run oil demand is so inelastic that a small supply loss causes a disproportionately large price spike
thinEvidence.note: Estimates of short-run oil demand elasticity cluster near -0.1, so a supply cut of a few percent implies a price move of tens of percent.

thinEvidence.text: Steel tariffs boosted domestic steel investment and jobs at only a small cost in higher steel prices
thinEvidence.note: The USITC found the Section 232 tariffs raised domestic steel output and prices modestly, but the same report found larger output losses in steel-using industries.

thinEvidence.text: US stock markets have set repeated record highs since the 2024 election [2026]
thinEvidence.note: Several autumn 2026 sources describe equities at or near record levels.

thinEvidence.text: The US strategic petroleum reserve is too depleted to keep offsetting supply losses [autumn 2026]
thinEvidence.note: The SPR fell below 300 million barrels, its lowest since the 1980s, which constrains but does not end releases.

thinEvidence.text: US strategic reserve releases and record exports cushioned Western fuel prices relative to Asia during the Hormuz closure
thinEvidence.note: US and Atlantic-basin supply is not routed through Hormuz, and SPR releases plus record exports added barrels, so Asian importers faced the tighter market.

thinEvidence.text: Tariff revenue and domestic investment offset the costs tariffs impose on consumers
thinEvidence.note: Rebating tariff revenue returns the transfer part of the cost, but Fajgelbaum et al. found the 2018-2019 tariffs still left a net loss after revenue because of deadweight and retaliation losses.

thinEvidence.text: Tariff revenue is far too small to offset the deficit increase from the 2025 tax cuts
thinEvidence.note: CBO scored the 2025 tax law at over $3 trillion of added deficits against tariff revenue of a few hundred billion a year.

thinEvidence.text: Tariff revenue is large enough to fund a cash payment to every adult citizen
thinEvidence.note: Tariffs bring in roughly 300-400 billion dollars a year while a 5,000 dollar payment to about 260 million adults would cost about 1.3 trillion dollars.

thinEvidence.text: Tariff revenue is small relative to federal interest costs and the deficit
thinEvidence.note: Tariffs raised roughly $200-300 billion a year against about $1.2 trillion of interest and a near-$2 trillion deficit.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs on Brazilian goods are the main cause of the recent spike in US beef and coffee prices [early 2026]
thinEvidence.note: The 50 percent Brazil tariff added to coffee and beef costs, but coffee was already up sharply on Brazilian drought and beef on a cyclically small US cattle herd and import restrictions.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs cut the trade deficit and boosted GDP [spring 2025]
thinEvidence.note: Imports fell in Q2 2025 after Q1 front-running, lifting measured GDP that quarter, but the 2025 goods deficit ended about equal to 2024.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs are driving a wave of domestic factory construction
thinEvidence.note: Some announced reshoring is real, but manufacturing employment fell in 2025 and tariff-exposed industries grew more slowly than lightly tariffed ones.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs and energy shocks that keep inflation elevated push long-term Treasury yields and mortgage rates higher
thinEvidence.note: Nominal long yields embed expected inflation, so policies that raise expected inflation raise borrowing costs, though how much of the 2026 yield rise is tariff-driven is contested.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs have hurt farmers by lowering crop prices and raising fertilizer costs
thinEvidence.note: Chinese retaliation collapsed US soybean exports in 2025 and tariffs on imported fertilizer raised input costs, both documented in USDA data.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs have not changed China's trade practices
thinEvidence.note: China did not meet its Phase One purchase commitments and expanded industrial subsidies and export volumes after 2018.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs have not reduced the overall US trade deficit [2025]
thinEvidence.note: The 2025 goods deficit was roughly unchanged at about $1.2 trillion as trade shifted from China to Mexico and Asia.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs have slowed US economic growth [2025]
thinEvidence.note: Forecasters cut 2025 growth after the tariffs and business investment weakened, but actual output held up better than expected, so the drag was real but modest.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs have triggered a record wave of factory construction in the US [2026]
thinEvidence.note: Manufacturing construction spending peaked in 2024 on CHIPS and IRA projects and has since declined, and manufacturing employment fell through 2025; pledges are not spending.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs hit low-margin cheap goods hardest, so they fall disproportionately on lower-income shoppers
thinEvidence.note: Tariffs are regressive because lower-income households spend a larger share on tradable goods and discount sellers have no margin to absorb duties.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs invite retaliatory tariffs from trading partners
thinEvidence.note: Every major US tariff round since 2018 drew matching retaliation from China, the EU, Canada and others.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs lead foreign manufacturers to build plants in the US to avoid them
thinEvidence.note: Tariff-jumping investment is a real mechanism (Japanese auto plants in the 1980s), but announced pledges far exceed realized spending and tariffs on inputs deter other investment.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs lower real wages because they raise prices without raising the revenue firms could use for pay rises
thinEvidence.note: Tariffs do reduce real incomes as a cost-push shock, but protected domestic producers gain revenue and nominal wages are not literally frozen.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs do not slow economic growth
thinEvidence.note: Most estimates put the 2025 tariffs at a drag of roughly half a point of GDP; no recession followed but growth was lower than otherwise.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs are now a major source of federal revenue
thinEvidence.note: Customs receipts ran about 30 billion dollars a month in late 2025, roughly 5 percent of federal revenue and several times the pre-2025 level.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs persist for decades once imposed because protected industries lobby to keep them
thinEvidence.note: The 1964 truck tariff still stands and the 2018 tariffs were kept by the next administration; concentrated beneficiaries defend them.

thinEvidence.text: Tariffs used briefly as bargaining leverage do far less harm than tariffs kept as long-run policy
thinEvidence.note: Prolonged protection compounds the losses, but 2018-2019 studies found trade-policy uncertainty itself cut investment even when tariffs were short-lived or merely threatened.

thinEvidence.text: Trade partners will keep their tariff deals despite the Supreme Court ruling [2026]
thinEvidence.note: Many partners signalled they would keep their deals, but the EU froze implementation of its side after the ruling.

thinEvidence.text: The EU's VAT acts like a tariff on US exports
thinEvidence.note: VAT applies equally to domestic and imported goods and is rebated on exports, so it does not discriminate against US products.

thinEvidence.text: Wage averages hide that low-income workers fare worse during inflation
thinEvidence.note: In 2021-24 low-wage workers saw the fastest real gains; in 2026 production workers' real pay fell slightly more than the average.

thinEvidence.text: When inflation outruns wages, workers demand raises that push prices up further in a wage-price spiral
thinEvidence.note: The mechanism exists, but post-2021 evidence shows spirals are rare when expectations stay anchored and labor bargaining power is weak.

thinEvidence.text: Withdrawal of war-risk insurance can halt tanker traffic even where ships could physically pass
thinEvidence.note: Tankers cannot sail uninsured, and Joint War Committee listings with 72-hour cancellation have stopped traffic in the Red Sea and Black Sea in recent years.

thinEvidence.text: Without Fed accommodation, tariffs cause layoffs because nominal wages do not fall
thinEvidence.note: Downward nominal wage rigidity is well documented, so a real-income cut that is not absorbed by prices shows up in hiring and employment.

thinEvidence.text: A worldwide trade war reduces international trade and leaves every country worse off
thinEvidence.note: Retaliatory tariff rounds in the 1930s and 2018-2019 cut trade volumes and produced net losses for both sides in the studies that measured them.
